                                         KEVIN KENNEDY’S
               REPLY EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

        Kevin Kennedy ("Mr. Kennedy”), a pro se intervenor, respectfully files these Reply

Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) pursuant to the PUC OPDM memorandum filed

on August 20, 2026.

        Mr. Kennedy makes this reply to Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC’s (“Oncor’s”)

and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s (“LCRA’s”)(collectively, “Applicants’ ”)

curious assertions that “The term “current county tax rolls” is undefined, and no evidence

establishes that the data Applicants used was not current.” 1 and that “The PFD must be wholly

rejected as contrary to sound electric system dynamics and planning.” 2 Mr. Kennedy asserts

that the term “current county tax rolls” is clearly understood by any reasonable person as

mandatory instruction to identify the current owners of affected properties at the time of

application, not whoever may have owned the property 3, 6, 12 or 15 months prior to application.

Additionally, the Applicants seem to have forgotten they previously provided the evidence that

they used old “tax card” data. 3

        With respect to need, it is actually the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) which must

be rejected as contrary to sound electric system dynamics and planning. Mr. Kennedy provides

additional evidentiary record references that strengthen the evidence that the Applicants failed to

establish the project is needed; the PBRP model is flawed for reliability and / or economics.

        The information presented below has been previously introduced into the record. Mr.

Kennedy does not seek to introduce new evidence, he does, however, ask the Honorable

Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) to take another, deeper look at portions of the evidence.

    I. THE APPLICANTS USED “TAX CARD” DATA FOR APPLICATION NOTICE
      THAT WAS NOT CURRENT:

           a. What does “current” mean and what is the intent of 16 TAC §22.52(a)(3).
                       Black’s Law Dictionary defines “current” as: “Running; now in transit;
               whatever is at present in course of passage; as ‘the current month.’” It also
               defines it in the temporal sense as: “Passing in time or belonging to the time
               actually passing, now passing, present in its course…”; however, Black’s
               cautions that the meaning of “current” depends largely upon the word it modifies
               and the subject matter with which it is associated.

                       The intent of requiring use of “current county tax rolls” in 16 TAC
               §22.52(a)(3) can reasonably be assumed to be a requirement that the notice of
               application be mailed to the current and actual owner of affected properties on the
               date the application is filed. It would seem unreasonable to argue it means
               anything else or that the parties lack the sophistication to interpret the meaning
               and intent.

                       The most up to date owner address information is, as required by
               §22.52(a)(3), the live, continuously updated, current county tax rolls as
               maintained in the county Central Appraisal District (CAD) offices. It is NOT the
               online “tax cards” used by the Applicants, which are simply annual snapshots
               taken of CAD records certified for annual property tax notice purposes that are
               not maintained to be current. The “current” tax roll data is the continuously
               updated GIS files. Use of the “tax cards” results in the potential to mail notices to
               a party that may have sold a property 12-18 months prior, which is what the
               Applicants did, and conversely, potential failure to notify a landowner party who
               may have bought a property 12-18 months prior.

                       Another caveat or issue raised is how much time is reasonably defensible
               as necessary for the Applicants to finalize preparation of the notices after they
               obtain mailing address information from the county appraisal districts, who
               maintain the current county tax rolls.




KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                          Page 3 of 18
                          Needing one week to finalize notices would seem defensible. Asking for
                 one month to finalize notices, considering the tremendous resources of the
                 Applicants, would seem a stretch, but is possibly forgivable. Trying to claim you
                 do not know the meaning of the word “current” and asserting utilization of tax
                 data that was over 15 months old is perfectly fine, is ludicrous by any standard.

            b. The Applicants’ screen captures tell it all.
                         The Applicants’ own response to Anna Thornton’s First Request for
                 Information (59475-5768), which Mr. Kennedy filed as admitted exhibit JKK
                 PANEL EX 10, in addition to the application itself, contain the evidence that
                 “establishes that the data Applicants used was not current.”

                         verifies that the Bell County Appraisal District informed her that “the
                         mapping is updated continuously throughout the year.” 4 This is standard
                         practice of county Central Appraisal Districts (CADs).

                         which the Applicant used to “verify” property ownership following
                         multiple landowner complaints due to lack of notice. Her attached “tax

                         CADs to be current.
                    iii. In the application, the Applicants again describe their reliance on these

                         noted: “*Supplemental address based on returned notice from public
                         meeting and additional tax card research” 7. They clearly relied on the
                         old online “tax card” data rather than obtaining current property owner
                         address information directly from the CADs’ live, continuously updated,

                  xiv. The evidentiary record is rife with other examples of the Applicants’
                       failure to properly notify landowners, but I will not continue and beat a
                       dead horse, as the record is clear: the Applicants DID NOT USE
                       CURRENT COUNTY TAX ROLLS for the mailing of notifications of
                       application.


           c. Additional Findings of Fact under “Notice of the Application”.
                       Under §2003.049(g), the Commission must adhere to the
               recommendations of the PFD unless the Commission finds that Administrative
               Law Judges (ALJs) misapplied the law or if the ALJs’ finding of fact is not
               supported by a preponderance of the evidence. Further, §2003.049(h) requires the
               Commission to state in writing the specific reason and legal basis for its
               determinations under subsection (g).

                       As such, Mr. Kennedy requests that the Honorable ALJs add the following
               Findings of Fact, to fortify the Proposal for Decision (PFD), and assure there is a
               preponderance of irrefutable evidence that the Applicants did not comply with 16
               TAC §22.52(a)(3).

                       XX. Bell Central Appraisal District (CAD) updates property ownership on
                       a continuous basis.

                       XX. Online CAD “tax cards” are not the continuously updated, current
                       county tax rolls maintained by CAD.

                       XX. Applicants relied on online CAD “tax cards” to develop notification
                       address lists and did not obtain current county tax rolls from CAD.

                       XX. Tract 3276 had been subdivided into about 25 residential lots on 9-3-
                       2024 by BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2.

                       XX. Beginning 12-12-2024, BWH Holdings LLC – Series 2 sold several
                       lots, including what later became 3276.2 and 3276.6.

                        XX. On 3-26-2026 date of application, Applicants were unaware BWH
                       Holdings LLC – Series 2 had subdivided the Tract 3276 almost 19 months
                       prior.

                       XX. On 3-26-2026 date of application, Applicants were unaware BWH
                       Holdings LLC – Series 2 had begun selling lots on 12-12-2024 and was
                       not the current owner of several lots on 3-26-2026.

                       XX. Because Applicants did not use current county tax rolls, Applicants
                       did not mail notice of application to Brandon Whatley Homes, LLC even
                       though Brandon Whatley Homes, LLC had purchased directly affected
                       Tract 3276.6 in 12-12-2024, almost 16 months prior to application.

                       XX. Applicants did not mail notice of their application to the owners of
                       land, as stated in the current county tax rolls, who would be directly
                       affected by the requested certificate, as required by 16 TAC §22.52(a)(3).

                       XX. The Application should be denied because Applicants failed to
                       comply with 16 Texas Administrative Code § (Rule) 22.52(a)(3) for
                       notice.



   II. THE PBRP RECOMMENDATIONS CANNOT BE TRUSTED:

           a. The PBRP modeled a spatially and temporally asymmetric distribution of
              load and generation.
                       It is irrefutable that the topology model(s) used for the PBRP employed a
               systemwide power-flow network in which ERCOT selectively updated TSP load
               demand, principally within the Permian Basin, but excluded similar known TSP
               load growth outside the Permian, though consideration of TSP loads was
               mandated by HB 5066.

                       From the PBRP:
                       “Summing the S&P Global forecast with the TDSP-provided load
               forecasts, the total demand in the Permian Basin region ERCOT has modeled in


KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                        Page 8 of 18
                  its studies for 2030 is 23,659 MW, and the total demand modeled for 2038 is
                 26,400 MW.
                          ERCOT also anticipates significant load growth outside the Permian
                 Basin region. TDSP load forecasts for the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan
                 (RTP) have identified approximately 59,400 MW of additional demand across the
                 ERCOT System that will need to be served by 2030.” 16

                          ERCOT seems to acknowledge that HB 5066 required that they use all
                 TSP load demand, even though they did not do that:

                          “As directed by HB 5066, the loads to be evaluated in this study would
                 include the following:
                          a. Load levels forecasted in the 2022 S&P Global Permian Basin study;
                          b. Load currently served by temporary on-site generation not already
                 accounted for in the S&P Global Permian Basin study;
                          c. Additional load currently seeking interconnection that is not otherwise
                 included in a or b, as determined by the electric utility with the responsibility for
                 serving the load. This should expressly include demand yet to sign a full
                 interconnection agreement.” 17
                          Compounding the selective load demand, ERCOT selectively updated
                 modeled future generation throughout the entire ERCOT system, placing it
                 primarily in area east of Interstate 35, as depicted in Figure 1. 18

                          Because modeled transmission flows are determined by the spatial or
                 geographical relationship between generation and load inputs entered into the
                 model by ERCOT, this selective asymmetric treatment reasonably could have
                 created artificial generation surpluses in Central / East Texas, which therefore
                 would have reasonably resulted in artificial east-to-west modeled power transfer
                 flows from the east into the Permian.

                          In the PBRP, ERCOT says that because of the extremely high Permian
                 load, “both the 2030 and 2038 PBRP power-flow base cases were initially not

                    solvable.” 19 ERCOT states they added the loads incrementally, identified
                   violations, added transmission, and then repeated the process. That methodology
                   may be reasonable for determining local transmission needs, but it creates a
                   potentially different issue when ERCOT uses the resulting case(s) to determine
                   regional import “requirements”.

                            ERCOT’s subsequent 2024- and 2025-RTP results—which identify
                   substantial Central Texas load growth and increasing Central Texas import
                   requirements—provide independent evidence that the Central Texas source/sink
                   conditions assumed by the PBRP were materially and substantially different from
                   ERCOT's later, more comprehensive planning cases.

                            From the 2025-RTP:
                            “Similar to the 2023 and 2024 RTPs, the 2025 RTP assessment results
                   highlighted the ongoing need for major import pathway enhancements to the
                   Central Texas corridor.” 20
                            If ERCOT’s objective was to determine how much power must (or could)
                   be transferred from the rest of the ERCOT system into the Permian, then the
                   loading conditions in the various potential source regions becomes just as
                   important as the load conditions in the Permian region. Disregarding the new TSP
                   load forecasts outside the Permian would reasonably create an unreliable model,
                   especially from a long-haul import perspective.

                            The available ERCOT evidentiary documentation establishes that the
                   PBRP and 2024-RTP were developed concurrently but from materially different
                   load-model vintages. The PBRP started with the 2023-RTP case and selectively
                   incorporated new TSP-provided loads at the bus level, but only those in the
                   Permian Basin region, while ERCOT's contemporaneous 2024-RTP process
                   incorporated a much larger statewide TSP load forecast.

                           From the PBRP:

                          “The 2023 RTP case, published on the Market Information System (MIS)
                 in October 2023, was used as the starting case in this study.” 21

                          “In addition to the S&P Global Permian Basin load forecast, the TSPs
                 relevant to the area also provided ERCOT the additional non-oil and gas loads
                 in the Permian Basin region to be included in this study.” 22

                               “ERCOT also anticipates significant load growth outside the Permian
                 Basin region. TDSP load forecasts for the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan
                 (RTP) have identified approximately 59,400 MW of additional demand across
                 the ERCOT System that will need to be served by 2030.” 23

                          Consequently, the PBRP apparently combined a then current (2024 TSP)
                 highly concentrated Permian load forecast with an older (2023) representation of
                 much lower loads elsewhere within the ERCOT system. Because ERCOT's
                 determination of Permian import requirements depends on the relative spatial
                 distribution of generation and load throughout the ERCOT system, this modeling
                 methodology presents a legitimate engineering concern as to whether the PBRP
                 case(s) overstated the east-to-west power transfer by greatly understating
                 forecasted load in the source areas outside the Permian, due to a failure to
                 consider contemporaneous (2024 TSP) load forecasts system wide.

                          As a result, not only should ERCOT’s PBRP not be given “great weight”
                 but it should be considered a flawed and statutorily invalid study and everything
                 that flows from it should be consider fruit of the poison tree, including all five
                 PBRP import path CCN dockets that relied solely on the PBRP for justification of
                 need, those being PUC Dockets 59029, 59182, 59315, 59336, and 59475.

                b. Spatial Distribution of Added Generation in PBRP (17,170-MW) and 2024-
                  RTP (59,200-MW) indicates high probability of questionable results.
                            The figures on the following page are graphical representations of
                   ERCOT’s spatial distribution generation of the added future generation required
                   to satisfy the demand forecast in the PBRP (Appendix A.1) 24 and the 2024-RTP
                   (Appendix B) 25. It is apparent even to the “layest” of lay persons that the
                   additional demand selected only in the Permian, combined with the selected
                   cluster of generation on the east end of Import Path 2, could yield a “modeled”
                   power flow from Bell County East to Sand Lake. However, that east-to-west flow
                   is not readily apparent in the load / generation distribution of 2024-RTP, where all
                   loads and all generation is considered, especially the added generation in the
                   Permian.

                            These maps provide a visual for the stark contrast between the input
                   ERCOT selected for the two models, which in theory should have represented
                   ERCOT’s best engineering efforts to develop a predictive model of a single
                   anticipated future condition, and not two totally different models.

                             Even a lay person can look at the two figures and immediately recognize
                   they are not the same. ERCOT created two entirely different 2030 models
                   alongside one another and thereby presented to the Commission two entirely
                   different simulations of the future.

                            The Applicants may try to argue that the PBRP was a regional plan, but
                   that does not mean it did not require a true and accurate system-wide model to
                   identify the true and accurate needs of the Permian region; it did in fact need a
                   complete model to accurately simulate future conditions.

                            The Applicants may argue ERCOT did not have enough time to do it right,
                   but that would be an absurd position. If ERCOT needed more time to properly
                   model expected future conditions, ERCOT should have asked for more time.
                   Texans should be able to expect that a State agency or its affiliate would never
                   release a flawed study.

                            The Applicants may argue Mr. Kennedy should be ignored because they
                   characterize him as a lay person, but SOAH Order No. 1 stated Mr. Kennedy had
                   a duty to bring this information forward. Likewise, the ALJs and Commissioners
                   have a duty to consider this information. Mr. Kennedy is a recently retired
                   professional engineer, who was responsible for projects requiring flow models of
                   a generally similar nature; he has sufficient engineering experience to recognize
                   inherent flaws in an asymmetric model.

                            Two months after submitting the PBRP, ERCOT themselves admitted it
                   was not a reliable study. In a letter to the Commission dated September 20, 2024,
                   ERCOT Vice President, Ms. Katie Hobbs stated: “Upon further internal
                   evaluation, however, ERCOT now believes that identifying the specific
                   transmission facility elements that could be utilized for either 345-kV or 765-kV
                   import options would require further engineering study by ERCOT's planning
                   department, which could result in additional delay of at least several months.” 26

                            In the Application, HB 5066 and the PBRP are the sole basis of need for
                   Import Path 2. ERCOT violated HB 5066 in developing the PBRP because they


26
     Hobbs letter to PUC (55718-46)

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                           Page 14 of 18
                    did not consider all the TSP load forecasts. They ignored all TSP load forecasts
                   outside the Permian Basin, relying on old 2023 load forecasts for the majority of
                   the system-wide model. This created a spatially and temporally inaccurate model
                   that could not yield accurate results.

                            Even though ERCOT admitted the PBRP was deficient and that “import
                   options would require further engineering study by ERCOT's planning
                   department” 27, the Applicants irrationally but boldly proclaim, “The PFD’s
                   disregard of years of independent transmission planning by the foremost experts
                   in the industry in favor of the hearsay, opinion testimony, and for the bald
                   assertions of lay witnesses is not only contrary to the Commission’s rules, it is
                   just short of ludicrous.” 28

                            If the ERCOT folks that built the PBRP model, --- which had a mishmash
                   of user selected, asymmetric load and generation inputs---, are “the foremost
                   experts in the industry”, we are in a world of hurt. If a random “lay” cedar
                   chopper from Mahomet knows more about structuring a trustworthy flow model
                   than the PUC, we need to reevaluate the statues and codes that have led us to this
                   point.

                            The Applicants hitched their application wagon to only HB 5066 and the
                   flawed PBRP. The ALJs’ PFD was spot on, except it did not include the full
                   record of insurmountable facts.


               c. Additional Findings of Fact under “Need for Import Path 2 - HB 5066 and
                   the Permian Basin Reliability Plan”.

                            Under §2003.049(g), the Commission must adhere to the
                   recommendations of the PFD unless the Commission finds that Administrative
                   Law Judges (ALJs) misapplied the law or if the ALJs’ finding of fact is not
                   supported by a preponderance of the evidence. Further, §2003.049(h) requires the

                Commission to state in writing the specific reason and legal basis for its
               determinations under subsection (g).

                       As such, Mr. Kennedy requests that the Honorable ALJs add the following
               Findings of Fact, to fortify the Proposal for Decision (PFD), and assure there is a
               preponderance of irrefutable evidence that the Applicants and the PBRP did not
               establish the need for Import Path 2, or any of the import paths for that matter.



                       XX. The PBRP only considered HB 5066 required TSP load forecasts that
                       were located in the Permian Basin.

                       XX. The PBRP did not consider HB 5066 required TSP load forecasts that
                       were located outside the Permian Basin.

                       XX. ERCOT selected 17,170-MW of added future generation, necessary
                       to meet the load demand, to the PBRP topology model.

                       XX. The majority of the added generation in the PBRP was located east of
                       Interstate 35.

                       XX. The 2024-RTP was developed concurrently with the PBRP.

                       XX. The 2024-RTP considered all HB 5066 required TSP load forecasts,
                       both inside and outside the Permian Basin.

                       XX. The 2024-RTP had approximately 45,000-MW of additional TSP
                       load demand versus the PBRP TSP load demand.
